doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: Folk tunes from North Korea, Indian rhythms and 'New Math'
summary: Fleck says folk music everywhere is similar and easy to learn. The hard work was Indian rhythmic formulas with Sandip Burman and layering rhythms in 'New Math' with Future Man.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I really enjoyed a couple of things on “Live Art” that stuck out. When you nailed — there’s a vocal tune on there, “O Darlin’” and when you nailed that six-eight groove, and then, later on in the CD you start playing a folk song from North Korea. To me that’s like, well this man has heard and absorbed an awful lot of music.

Well I love music but to me it’s more all similar than it is different. It’s not that — I mean a great folk tune from the United States and a great folk tune from North Korea aren’t that different. And when you hear this version of it you can hear that pretty clearly. Like that Korean tune is a simple pentatonic tune and we have tons of them here so it’s just a different tune. You’re just learning the tune. It’s not — I mean there are things that we’ve done that I think are like an achievement and for me like on “Live Art” — not “Live Art” on “Live at the Quick,” practicing and working with Sandip Burman on Indian formulas to come up with this and rhythms that come out that were correct in an Indian rhythmic structure, that took a lot of hard work. That didn’t follow the folk patterns or the bluegrass patterns or the jazz patterns or the things that I understood. You know what I mean? Or things like there’s a piece on the last album that Future Man and I wrote together called “New Math” that involved laying different rhythmic structures on top of other structures. Like playing in four-four but then superimposing a five on top of it, really, really fast, and then superimpose, then going up to six, seven, eight over that same rhythm while keeping the basic pulse the same. That took some work. But learning some beautiful folk tunes in different countries, that happened fast. It was easy, it was natural as it could be, and it was really fun.
And it’s a nice sort of release when it comes in the record I think.
Yeah, I think it just shows up — there’s just beautiful music everywhere. It’s just part of listening and checking it out.
